extracted.intended_audience: journal peer reviewers of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (content experts and methodologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing peer review of completed systematic reviews and meta-analyses (and protocols), covering what to check (methods, reporting, statistics), how to structure the review, when to decline, and which reporting guidelines to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify reviewer role and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers should initially assess whether the journal has approached them as a content expert, methodologist, or both, and check for obvious conflicts of interest (e.g., by reviewing the abstract and author list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invited as a methodologist, minimize time spent commenting on content; if as a content expert, expect to address both content and methods. Quickly screen for conflicts and inform the editor if help (e.g., from a mentor) was used to complete the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reporting guideline checklists (EQUATOR/PRISMA and extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement any journal-provided peer review template with an appropriate reporting guideline checklist (e.g., PRISMA, PRISMA-P, PRISMA-IPD, PRISMA extension for network meta-analysis, MOOSE, ENTREQ, RAMESES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine checklist items to jog memory about required reporting elements; use the EQUATOR Network library to identify the right guideline. The PRISMA explanation and elaboration documents are useful background for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start the review with a brief summary (précis) of Methods and Results
rubrics_metrics.description: A good peer review begins with a short paragraph summarizing what the authors performed (Methods) and found (Results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The précis demonstrates the reviewer has grasped the salient aspects and orients authors/editors; follow the summary by positive comments before criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with positives, then present major/fatal flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: After the summary, mention positive aspects of the manuscript, then focus on any major problems or fatal flaws detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of positives (topical issue, well-documented eligibility criteria). Present major problems as questions for clarification rather than accusations. Fatal examples include reliance on personal files instead of a systematic search or lack of risk-of-bias assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pose criticisms as questions and seek clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Present problems and potential methodological concerns as questions to the authors rather than accusatory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may have simply omitted reporting; framing concerns as queries allows authors to explain or correct omissions and keeps tone constructive and professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise, evidence-based, and professional in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the peer review to approximately one single-spaced, double-sided page (~1000 words), be as evidence-based as possible, and avoid rudeness or unnecessary personal opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support substantive comments with references when possible (e.g., evidence about risk-of-bias effects). Limit personal opinion and never be rude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check completeness and peer review of search strategy (PRESS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the authors clearly reported their search strategy and whether that search strategy underwent any peer review (eg, PRESS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for peer review of the search, reproduce/inspect the search strategy for errors, and ask for clarification if the search is poorly reported or missing; Sampson et al.'s PRESS guidance can help identify common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess risk-of-bias appraisal of included studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the authors assessed risk of bias in the included studies and whether appropriate methods were used and reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If risk-of-bias assessments are absent or inadequate, ask authors why and request appropriate assessments; cite evidence that inadequate reporting (eg, randomization) can exaggerate effect estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess potential outcome reporting bias against protocol/registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Check for selective outcome reporting by comparing the review's reported outcomes to those documented in the protocol or registration (e.g., PROSPERO or published protocol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a PROSPERO registration number or published protocol is provided, compare planned vs reported outcomes; if discrepancies exist, seek explanation from authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a separate statistical/methods section for meta-analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a review includes one or more meta-analyses, devote a separate section of the peer review to statistical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the authors indicated the statistical approach (fixed-effects, random-effects, Bayesian), reported point estimates with confidence intervals, and assessed publication bias (graphical methods and statistical tests such as Egger). Ask for sufficient detail so analyses can be replicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requesting authors to conduct a new review
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not ask authors to make changes that amount to performing a new systematic review (e.g., substantially changing eligibility criteria or adding different study designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such substantial modifications are often unhelpful; if the manuscript's scope/methods are fundamentally flawed, confidentially recommend rejection to the editor rather than instructing authors to redo the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess discussion for spin and reporting of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the discussion overstates results (spin) or appropriately addresses limitations of the review and the included studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek clarification when the discussion appears overly optimistic; ask that authors explicitly report limitations of their review and limitations of included evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to decline (specialized review types/statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept to review reports requiring methods you are unfamiliar with (e.g., network meta-analyses, individual participant data meta-analyses, advanced statistical approaches, or complex mixed-methods designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRISMA has extensions for many specialized designs; if you lack competence, inform the editor and decline rather than provide superficial comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PRISMA-P for peer reviewing protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: When invited to peer review a systematic review protocol, use the PRISMA-P checklist to assess completeness of planned methods and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare protocol content to PRISMA-P items and suggest clarifications or additions to ensure transparency and reproducibility of the planned review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement journal template with checklist items and explanation documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a journal provides a review template, use reporting checklists and their explanation/elaboration documents to ensure thorough coverage of required items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRISMA explanation and elaboration and other guideline E&Es explain why specific information should be included and can help reviewers identify omitted or inadequately reported items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be familiar with recent literature and prior reviews in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective peer reviewers should be aware of recent advances and other reviews in the topic area to judge novelty, comprehensiveness, and appropriateness of citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relevant recent reviews are omitted, ask authors to explain why their study was undertaken and to cite or contrast with prior work; this helps detect omissions and justifies the review's contribution.
